title: Lifetime Earnings and the Vietnam Era Draft Lottery: Evidence from Social Security Administrative Records
research_question: What is the long-term causal effect of military service during the Vietnam era on the civilian earnings of veterans, particularly years after their discharge? Do veterans suffer a persistent earnings penalty relative to comparable nonveterans, and if so, can this be explained by lost civilian labor market experience?
data_description: The primary earnings data come from the Social Security Administration's Continuous Work History Sample (CWHS), a one percent sample of Social Security numbers, providing annual FICA taxable earnings (1964-84) and W-2 total compensation (1978-84) for men born 1950-1953. A special extract matched dates of birth, allowing assignment of Random Sequence Numbers (RSNs, 1-365) from published Selective Service tables. Data are aggregated into cells defined by year of earnings, year of birth, race, and groups of five consecutive lottery numbers, reporting means, variances, and censoring fractions. Probabilities of veteran status are tabulated from the 1984 Survey of Income and Program Participation (Wave I, Panel I, ~20,000 households) and from Defense Manpower Data Center administrative accession records (July 1970-December 1973). Current Population Survey data are used to adjust for FICA censoring at the taxable maximum.
institutional_context: During the Vietnam War, the United States held five draft lotteries (1970-1975) covering men born 1944-1953. In a televised drawing, birthdates were assigned RSNs from 1 to 365, randomly determining priority for induction. Each year the Defense Department announced a draft-eligibility ceiling (RSN 195 in 1970, 125 in 1971, 95 in 1972), and only men with numbers below the ceiling could be drafted. The randomization meant draft-eligible and draft-ineligible men differed only in their conscription risk. Many men with low numbers volunteered to improve terms of service, and behavioral responses extended even to the 1953 cohort, which was never drafted. Pre-induction physical and mental tests further screened the eligible pool. No one was drafted after 1972, and conscription authority expired in July 1973, marking the transition to an All-Volunteer Force. Millions of veterans subsequently received GI benefits including education, housing, and medical care.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: IV — treatment = drafted individuals, control = non-drafted individuals; instrument = draft lottery number

key_variables.treatment: draft eligibility based on lottery number
key_variables.control: individuals not eligible for the draft based on lottery number

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Being drafted during the Vietnam War had a positive impact on lifetime earnings for those who served.
key_robustness: alternative specifications of the earnings model
